Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

issues.item: Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile: darkness and especially tactile/unexpected touch are more characteristic of direct interpersonal assault than of a loved-one trauma, and there is no accompanying memory or appraisal content that links touch or darkness to this trauma.

The lock-checking threat item and parallel checking-locks strategy suggest a home-intrusion or direct personal danger formulation. In a loved-one trauma profile, this can occur, but here it is not supported by any appraisals or memory content about preventing another loss, danger to family, or responsibility. As selected, these items pull toward a different trauma narrative than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Within the allowed nodes, the strongest coherence is around hyperarousal and intrusive memory, but the specific combination of tactile triggers plus lock-checking behavior is difficult to explain as one coherent formulation for a loved-one trauma without any linked negative appraisal content. This is more than merely unusual because the selected items imply different threat contexts.

The trigger/threat pattern is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of trauma to a loved one. Tactile unexpected-touch triggers plus broad startle to nearby movement are more typical of direct assault or personal threat trauma, not bereavement-focused trauma, unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Door/lock checking and hypervigilant startle responses imply an ongoing fear of intruders or immediate physical attack, but the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory and loss-related trigger content rather than a coherent physical-danger narrative tied to the loved-one trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, but the selected threat items reflect personal safety/intruder danger whereas the only clearly trauma-congruent trigger is loss-themed conversation. This creates a poor match between the active nodes: the threat content does not plausibly arise from the listed trauma-relevant triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, tactile triggering by unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a direct personal-assault or physical-threat theme that is not supported by the memory items or the loss-focused trigger item. This makes the trigger set clinically incoherent around the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window lock checking suggests an ongoing home-intrusion or personal safety threat appraisal. In a profile centered on trauma to a loved one, with memory items focused on reliving and no appraisals linking the event to current intruder danger, this threat item does not fit the dominant loss-based formulation and appears mismatched with the other selected items.

issues.item: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeatedly checking locks/doors/windows is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the indexed trauma type (trauma to a loved one). The other selected items center on grief/loss reminders, intrusive vivid replay, and generalized startle, but do not indicate a home-intrusion, assault, or safety-compulsion theme that would make lock-checking a coherent trauma-linked strategy. As selected, this item appears to target a threat-management pattern not otherwise represented in triggers, memory, or appraisals.

vignette:
Daniel is a 48-year-old shopowner who came to treatment more than a year after his wife's sister died violently, an event he had been pulled into at close range because he was the family member who identified the body and helped make the funeral arrangements. He still describes the day in fragments that are painfully sharp: the funeral home's fluorescent light, the stillness of her face, the scent of flowers and polished wood, his wife collapsing beside him. What stays with him is not only that she was gone, but the helplessness of being the one who had to look, confirm, and keep functioning while his wife was falling apart. Since then, anything tied to loss has become charged. If a customer in his store starts talking about someone who "lost their mom" or "buried a brother," Daniel feels his body tense before he can think. Passing a cemetery on the drive to work or hearing about a funeral in town can unsettle him for the rest of the day, and reminders of victims in the news or in conversation hit him with particular force because they pull him back toward the image of his sister-in-law's body.

What frightened Daniel early on was how suddenly ordinary moments could feel dangerous. A stock cart clattering in the back of the shop or someone stepping into his peripheral vision makes him jolt hard, his chest already braced as if something terrible is about to happen. In those moments the old scene comes back with unnerving force. He does not experience it as a sad memory he is choosing to recall; it is more like the room at the funeral home has opened again around him. The image is vivid and exact, and it replays "like a film," as he puts it, with details he wishes he could forget. Because he is already on edge, reminders of loss land harder: a grieving customer, a bouquet meant for a memorial, even the word "funeral" seems to leap out at him, and he scans for these cues almost automatically.

Over the months that followed, Daniel built his days around not setting any of this off. In the shop, if conversation turns toward death or bereavement, he finds a reason to walk into the storeroom or abruptly changes the subject. He has stopped attending funerals altogether and will not drive past the cemetery if there is any alternate route. At home, if his wife begins talking about her sister, he goes quiet, lights a cigarette, and steps outside rather than let himself think about that day. The same thing happens when the memory intrudes on its own: he reaches for a cigarette, focuses on small tasks, or pushes the thoughts away as if refusing them will keep him steady. His avoidance makes immediate sense to him because he is convinced that if he lets himself dwell on it, he will be pulled all the way back into those moments and lose control.

But the more Daniel has organized his life around not thinking and not feeling, the less settled he has become. Because he cuts off conversations about loss and steers clear of funerals, cemeteries, and other grief-related reminders, those situations have stayed raw and potent; they still hit him like something current rather than something survived. Pushing the images away has not weakened them. If anything, the memory returns more forcefully, highly detailed and present, especially after days when he has been trying hardest not to think about it. Smoking gives him a brief sense of relief, yet he notices that after stepping outside for a cigarette he often comes back even more tightly wound, more reactive to noise and sudden movement in the store, more likely to be set off by some mention of another family's loss. On bad days this pattern repeats several times before lunch.

The effect on his life has narrowed him. Daniel used to be the kind of owner who chatted easily with regulars; now his staff have noticed that he disappears when certain conversations start, and his wife experiences him as shut down whenever her sister is mentioned. He hates that, because part of him knows he is leaving her alone with her grief, yet what he feels most strongly is fear-fear of the surge of horror, guilt, and helplessness that comes if he lets the memory come fully into view. He sought help after startling violently when a customer dropped a box near the register and, seconds later, finding himself back in the funeral home so completely that he had to leave the floor. What he wants is not to erase his sister-in-law, but to be able to hear about loss, stand beside his wife, and walk through his own days without feeling as though the worst moment of his life is still happening now.
